newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cenbank says still too early for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Czech cenbank says still too early for rate cut.

text.p: The Czech National Bank said on Monday that inflation pressures do not permit a cut in interest rates soon, despite data released earlier in the day showing inflation slowing to its lowest level since 1993.

"No, no, no. Only after the central bank will be sure that inflation pressures are, I would say weaker, could it consider some changes in monetary policy, but this is not the case now," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said earlier that year-on-year inflation eased to 7.3 percent in February, down from 7.4 percent the previous month, and the moving 12-month average, which uses 1993 as a base, edged down to 8.6 percent compared with 9.1 percent in February 1996.

Analysts and the central bank attribute the inflation fall to a one percentage point rise in the discount rate last summer -- to 10.5 percent -- along with a rise in minimum reserve requirements which restricted the growth of the money supply significantly.
Several analysts on Monday said the positive results might cause the central bank to start thinking about a rate cut.
"But what we are afraid about is the gap in supply and demand. Demand rose by about nine percent (in 1996) and (GDP) growth by about four percent last year," Svehla said.

In the most recent published results, the Statistical Bureau said nine-month 1996 real GDP growth was four percent, year-on-year, while aggregate demand growth was just over five percent. Full-year 1995 figures are expected later this month.

But the economy has shown signs of slowing with third quarter growth at 3.6 percent. Meanwhile, the CNB's tightening slowed M2 money supply growth to under 10 percent by the end of the year from more than 20 percent in the first half.
"We are now, somewhere between eight and nine (percent M2 growth) year on year," Svehla said.

"The reasons for the fact that the growth of the economy is reduced are multi-dimensional, not only (central bank) monetary policy... I am cautious to deny that we affected (GDP) growth, but it can be only one reason, surely not the main reason."

Svehla said the CNB was waiting for more information on the government's plan to deregulate housing rents and energy prices, and the level of subsidies the government will provide to offset the increases for low-income families.

He said it was most important for the government, which is trying to stem the growth of a state budget deficit that reached 6.7 billion crowns by the end of February, to not only look at budget cuts, but a redistrubtion of spending.
"Cuts and restructuring this would be good. If the state budget would focus expenditure more on investments in economic potential and productivity of the labour force... this can help," he said.
